attributes.description:
Background: Social disconnection has been proposed as a contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis. However, it remains unclear how social disruptions reshape social networks and their links to mental wellbeing across age groups. The present study examined whether social disruptions (during the COVID-19 pandemic) reshape social networks and how changes in social networks differently relate to mental health and loneliness in adolescents compared to adults. 
Methods: The study used egocentric network analysis of data from 1,278 participants (88% female; aged 11-89 years, mean = 37.2±16.2 years) in the multinational (Australia, the U.K., and U.S.) prospective COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study. Social network properties of structural density, functional closeness, and interaction frequency were derived. Linear mixed-effects modelling was employed to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations with mental wellbeing at baseline, three-month, and six-month follow-up.
Results: Adolescents reported more virtual interactions, and less in-person contact. Greater network closeness was associated with lower depression, whereas dense but less close networks were linked to greater loneliness. Reduced contact from pre-pandemic levels were also linked to poorer wellbeing, particularly among younger individuals. 
Conclusions: The present findings highlight that age differences in social experiences, such as social network structure (density) and function (closeness and interaction frequency), may underlie young people’s greater mental health vulnerability during social disruptions. This underscores the importance of developing age-sensitive and context-responsive strategies to better support mental wellbeing during times of social disruption.
attributes.title: The Cost of Disconnection: Longitudinal Egocentric Network Analyses Linking Social Isolation to Loneliness and Mental Health in Adolescents and Adults

attributes.description: Despite age being a significant sociodemographic correlate of conspiratorial mentality, surprisingly little is known about its precursors and consequences among older people. Older people are often considered at risk of psychological distress, which often relates to conspiratorial mentality. Our study therefore assumed bidirectional relations between these constructs. Distress was represented by loneliness, anxiety, and depression. We also investigated potential moderation by social media use, as conspiracy theories tend to be disseminated on such media. We tested these associations linearly and quadratically using data from a two-wave longitudinal study of Czech adults aged 60+ (NW1 = 4133, MageW1 = 69.1). Conspiratorial mentality was not predicted by other variables, indicating that these are probably not risk factors for such mentality. Conversely, conspiratorial mentality positively predicted only anxiety. Social media use moderation and quadratic effects were unsupported. Overall, the study suggests that conspiratorial mentality can be an anxiety-provoking experience among older people.
attributes.title: Conspiratorial mentality among older people: The role of loneliness, depression, anxiety, and social media use

attributes.description: Polarization can be described as when opinions and attitudes discontinue existing on a continuum and are drawn to opposing extremes. Affective polarization refers to the positive feelings and associations towards one’s own political ingroup, in combination with negative feelings and associations that arise towards the outgroup on the other end of the spectrum. Recent studies have shown that polarization is increasing in several countries. This change is happening simultaneously with increases in singleness and loneliness. Moreover, a historically significant political gap can be observed in many Western countries between young men and women, raising questions regarding heterosexual relationship formation. The current study set out to examine differences in affective polarization in men and women, and to test loneliness, age, and relationship status as predictors of affective polarization in a Nordic multiparty democracy. We used a population-based sample of 7,357 Finnish adults who responded to an online survey. In line with previous findings, men were found more likely to be TAN (traditional-authoritarian-nationalist)-polarized, and women more likely to be GAL (green-alternative-libertarian)-polarized. In addition, polarization was found to be more common among younger respondents. Surprisingly, relationship status was not found to be a significant predictor of affective polarization. Loneliness was found to be more common in GAL-, but not in TAN-polarized respondents, indicating that less moderate political alignment may be associated with loneliness in general.
attributes.title: Divided Politics, Divided Lives? Affective Polarization, Gender, and Loneliness in Finland

attributes.description: We examine (1) whether indicators of early-life adversity are associated with children’s loneliness complaints and their recurrence at ages 5 and 9; and (2) whether children’s loneliness complaints are associated with poorer educational achievement measured at age 22 after adjusting for early-life adversity indicators. We used data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (US, original sample n=4,898; study sample n=2,456). Children’s loneliness complaints were reported by the principal caregiver. We applied (1) binomial logistic regression and (2) weighted g-computation. In our sample, 6.8% of children had recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints. Indicators of socioenvironmental early-life adversity were associated with higher odds of loneliness complaints. Moreover, higher material hardship and lower neighborhood collective efficacy were associated with higher odds of complaints recurring at ages 5 and 9. We observed no association between caregiver-reported loneliness in childhood and later educational achievement. We note limitations in our measurement of childhood loneliness.
attributes.title: Early-life adversity, childhood loneliness, and young adulthood educational achievement: a prospective study

attributes.description: Although interpersonal factors are implicated in theoretical models of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), little is known about how objective social context and subjective interpersonal experiences contribute to momentary NSSI urges and behaviors in clinical populations. The present study examined between- and within-person associations among several interpersonal processes (perceived rejection, perceived social support, social context, social context appraisals, loneliness) and NSSI urges and behavior in daily life. One-hundred-twenty-five treatment-seeking adolescents and adults with recent NSSI completed a 28-day Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) protocol with six daily surveys (15,098 assessments). Dynamic structural equation modeling examined between- and within-person contemporaneous and temporal associations. Higher perceived rejection at baseline predicted greater average NSSI urge intensity and NSSI behavior during the 28-day EMA period, whereas baseline perceived social support was unrelated to either outcome. Momentary objective social context (i.e., being alone versus with others) was not a robust predictor of NSSI urges or behavior in daily life. In contrast, more positive momentary appraisals of social contexts predicted prospective decreases in NSSI urge intensity across 2-hour intervals, while higher-than-usual momentary loneliness predicted within-person increases in both NSSI urge intensity and the likelihood of NSSI behavior. Fully prospective mediation analyses indicated that the temporal effects of loneliness and social context appraisals on NSSI behavior operated primarily through their effect on NSSI urges. Subjective interpersonal experiences, rather than objective social context, were consistently linked to short-term NSSI risk. Interventions targeting maladaptive social appraisals and loneliness, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, may help prevent NSSI urges and behavior in daily life.
attributes.title: Interpersonal Processes in Daily Life: Loneliness and Social Appraisals as Real-Time Predictors of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Urges and Behavior

attributes.description:
Background: For young people experiencing loneliness or low community connection, physical activity may support social contact, enjoyment and belonging. Social prescribing offers a person-centred route to organised sport, exercise, active recreation and less structured movement, but identification or referral does not ensure usability. Little is known about the individual, relational, school and community conditions that make these opportunities meaningful to the young person, workable within their circumstances and acceptable in their social and emotional context.
Methods: A targeted qualitative content analysis with iterative framework development used data from INcreasing AdolesCent social and community supporT (INACT), a school-based social prescribing programme for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection. 38 interviews were screened (12 young people, eight parents/guardians, five school staff and 13 link workers); 37 contained physical-activity material. These were analysed alongside link-worker records for 163 young people. Material was charted by activity category, setting, pathway stage, barriers and inclusion or emotional-safety considerations, then compared across pilot interviews, full-trial interviews and logs. Three researchers contributed to coding, checking and collective interpretation.
Results: Across interviews and routine records, physical-activity material encompassed organised sport, fitness and exercise, dance and creative movement, outdoor activity, informal movement or active recreation, and other community activities. Five overlapping areas of work were identified: understanding interests and personal fit; expanding activity options; supporting access and entry; working through practical feasibility and sustainability; and considering inclusion and emotional safety. These areas were not sequential and could overlap or be revisited. School settings interacted with family routines, peer cultures and community provision to shape usability. Logs more often documented named activities, practical actions and spending, whereas interviews provided fuller accounts of confidence, social fit and family constraints. Pathway stages from discussion and referral to attendance and continuation were not consistently distinguished.
Conclusion: For pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection, access to a potentially connecting physical activity depended on more than availability or referral. The framework describes the practical, relational and contextual work involved in moving towards meaningful, workable and acceptable participation. It locates responsibility across families, schools, providers, services and local infrastructure while keeping young people’s preferences and choices central. The study does not establish that physical activity reduced loneliness, but provides a basis for prospective evaluation of participation, social connection and loneliness outcomes.
attributes.title: Beyond referral: Making physical activity opportunities usable in school-based social prescribing for young people experiencing loneliness

attributes.description: Loneliness is a well-established risk factor for physical and mental health in later life. This work responds to recent calls to examine the dimensionality of the UCLA Loneliness Scale among older adults. In a preregistered secondary analysis using three measurement occasions from the publicly available National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project (NSHAP), we applied taxometric analyses (i.e., mean above minus below a cut, maximum eigenvalue, latent mode factor analysis, and comparison curve fit index) to examine the latent structure of the 3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale. Results supported the preregistered hypothesis, showing the mean comparison curve fit index (CCFI) was below 0.45 on each measurement occasion (CCFI range: 0.23 – 0.35). Therefore, loneliness, as measured in this sample, likely follows a continuous rather than categorical distribution, with no clear cut point. These findings inform statistical decision-making regarding loneliness classification and use of this scale in this sample.
attributes.title: A Taxometric Analysis of the Three-Item UCLA Loneliness Scale in the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project

attributes.description: Loneliness is a growing public health concern rooted in emotional distress and social disconnection. Interpersonal emotion regulation — managing ones’ own or others’ emotions — is a mechanism for strengthening social bonds and fostering emotional health. Their shared socio-emotional foundation raises the possibility that loneliness may be connected to how people regulate others and are regulated in turn. Accordingly, we investigated whether loneliness is associated with adaptive and maladaptive interpersonal emotion regulation strategies in the moment and over time. To address this question, we conducted a daily diary (N = 170, collected 2020; Study 1) and experience sampling study (N = 239, collected 2021; Study 2). Participants reported on global trait loneliness, then recorded momentary loneliness and use of four strategies as both regulator (regulating others extrinsically) and target of regulation (being regulated by others intrinsically) for seven days. State loneliness predicted greater invalidation as both regulator and target, and global trait loneliness predicted less physical support as regulator and target. Most consistently, the person-level average of momentary loneliness across the week predicted greater use of all strategies — responsiveness, invalidation, reappraisal, and physical support — both as regulator and target. Methodologically, our findings show the importance of assessing loneliness at different time scales. Theoretically, our findings suggest lonely individuals do actively attempt emotion regulation during interactions, yet they may be just as likely to use maladaptive strategies that undermine connection as adaptive strategies that enhance it. This work underscores the importance of interaction quality in understanding how loneliness persists and might be interrupted.
attributes.title: Loneliness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life

attributes.description: Loneliness, a subjective state of perceived social isolation characterized by chronic social hypervigilance, is a profound risk factor for physical and mental health conditions. While functional neuroimaging studies link loneliness to altered salience network connectivity, the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting lonely brain remain unexplored. We investigated the relationship between trait loneliness and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) microstates. Sixty-one healthy young adults completed the UCLA Loneliness Scale and Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and underwent 3-minute resting-state EEG recording. A criterion-based five-class microstate solution identified a topography corresponding to the canonical Class C/E, associated with both self-referential and salience-related processing. Higher loneliness scores were significantly associated with reduced Class C/E occurrence, which remained significant after controlling for depressive symptoms, age, and sex. Exploratory source localization revealed that lonelier individuals showed reduced current density in the middle cingulate cortex (MCC). These findings suggest that chronic social hypervigilance suppresses the spontaneous mobilization of the salience network at rest, with reduced MCC engagement reflecting a dispositional attenuation consistent with chronic relational threat.
attributes.title: Loneliness is reflected in the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting brain: an EEG microstate study

attributes.description: Chen et al. argued that shame and loneliness play a role in the longitudinal emergence of non-suicidal self-injury among adolescents. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Chen et al., we examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.
attributes.title: Questionable prospective effects between shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury among Chinese adolescents: A reassessment of Chen et al. (2026)

attributes.description: Understanding the psychosocial and community risk factors associated with financial exploitation is essential in developing prevention strategies. Although previous work has identified factors related to increased risk such as poor financial literacy, cognitive decline, and worse mental health, less is known about social factors, particularly those tied to our community and how they interact with our ability to form meaningful relationships. To investigate this issue, we used a previously published national sample of U.S. adults aged 20 to 94 (N = 886). We used self-reported zip code data coupled with the US Census data to reconstruct community-level indicators of social cohesion (i.e., neighborhood disorder, neighborhood disadvantage, residential instability). We found that reduced community-level social cohesion was associated with increased risk for financial exploitation. In addition, our exploratory analyses indicated that community-level indicators of social cohesion moderated the association between subjective cognitive decline and risk of financial exploitation. Specifically, individuals with higher levels of subjective cognitive decline residing in areas with low residential instability appeared to have lower risk of financial exploitation. These results highlight how community-level factors contribute to risk for financial exploitation, which may provide a foundation for future work aimed at improving prevention strategies and public policy.
attributes.title: Reduced Community-Level Social Cohesion is Associated with Higher Risk for Financial Exploitation

attributes.description:
This study proposes a systems approach to explore the entropy signatures of war phases
on social cohesion dynamics in Ukraine (2004-2025). Using a psycholinguistic time series of
online searches for first-person plural pronouns, we quantified social cohesion complexity using
sample entropy and refined composite multiscale entropy (RCMSE). Analyses reveal distinct
signatures between war phases over time for both metrics, with respectively R2 = 0.57
and R2 = 0.95. Relative to peace and full invasion, social cohesion entropy decreased under
partial invasion and displayed more anti-persistent behavior. While social cohesion was most
dysfunctional under partial invasion, entropy signatures of full-scale invasion and peace were
relatively close. These results offer insights into the impact of interstate aggression on social
cohesion and contribute to a thermodynamic understanding of warfare as a systemic shock.
The methodology provides a framework for monitoring and predicting societal resilience in
response to significant events.
attributes.title: Entropy signatures of interstate aggression on social cohesion dynamics

attributes.description: In his book “The Anxious Generation”, Jonathan Haidt suggests that digital technologies are rewiring children's brains and causing a mental illness epidemic. However, as noted by different colleagues, this claim is not supported by scientific evidence. In general, most available data are correlational, and when researchers find causal effects, they are small or inconclusive. As the debate on the neurodevelopmental impact of digital technologies persists, we introduce the "Disembodied Disconnect Hypothesis." This perspective posits that social media and digital platforms are fundamentally altering the landscape of human sociality without necessarily rewiring cognitive structures. We argue that while these technologies offer novel avenues for interaction and community-building, they significantly differ from traditional, embodied forms of social engagement. This disembodied nature of digital interactions may exacerbate existing social inequalities and mental health issues, particularly for those already struggling with loneliness and social anxiety.
attributes.title: The Disembodied Disconnect Hypothesis:  How Online Interactions Undermine Neurobiological Foundations of Social Cohesion

attributes.description: Past research has found intergroup contact to be a promising intervention to reduce prejudice and has identified adolescence as the developmental period during which intergroup contact is most effective. Few studies, however, have tested whether contact-based interventions can be scaled up to improve intergroup relations at a large scale. The present research evaluated whether and when the National Citizen Service, a large-scale contact-based intervention reaching one in six 15- to 17-year-olds in England and Northern Ireland, builds social cohesion among adolescents from different ethnic backgrounds. In a diverse sample of adolescents (N = 2,099; M = 16.37, age range: 15–17 years; 58% female), this study used a pretest–posttest design with a double pretest to assess the intervention’s effectiveness. Controlling for test–retest effects, this study found evidence that the intervention decreased intergroup anxiety and increased outgroup perspective-taking—but not that it affected intergroup attitudes, intergroup trust, or perceptions of relative (dis )advantage. These (small) effects were greater for adolescents who had experienced less positive contact before participating and who talked more about group differences while participating. These findings suggest that the intervention might not immediately improve intergroup relations—but that it has the potential to prepare adolescents, especially those with less positive contact experiences before the intervention, for more positive intergroup interactions in the future.
attributes.title: Building social cohesion through intergroup contact: Evaluation of a large-scale intervention to improve intergroup relations among adolescents

attributes.description: In many contexts, direct gaze is regarded as a socially rewarding signal that promotes positive interpersonal evaluations, yet most evidence stems from single, in-the-moment judgments of briefly presented faces. Across three eye-tracking experiments, we examined whether repeated gaze-contingent interactions shape more enduring social evaluations. Participants repeatedly exchanged gaze with a few on-screen virtual partners who reciprocated their gaze with systematically different probabilities. Afterwards, participants estimated gaze reciprocity rates for each partner and completed several ratings (e.g., feelings of social connectedness, social agency). Notably, participants reliably distinguished between gaze reciprocity rates of interaction partners even when differences in actual gaze reciprocity were small and close to chance (40% vs. 60%), though estimates were compressed toward the middle of the range. Critically, while objective gaze reciprocity rates showed little consistent relation to social evaluations, subjectively perceived reciprocity rates were robustly associated with social connectedness and social agency across experiments. Additionally, some experiments pointed to associations with likability and trust (entrusted money in an economic Trust Game). However, these associations did not extend to implicit behavioral measures (free-choice gaze selection, gaze cueing). A pooled multilevel mediation analysis confirmed that objective gaze reciprocity rates predicted connectedness indirectly, via subjective perception. Together, these findings suggest that social evaluation is shaped more by the experience of being looked at than by objective gaze reciprocity itself, at least when gaze reciprocity levels are somewhat difficult to differentiate.
attributes.title: Experienced vs. actual gaze reciprocity in repeated social interactions: A gateway toward social connectedness

attributes.description: Chronotype refers to individual preferences regarding the timing of activity and rest within the circadian cycle. Previous research has demonstrated its associations with various aspects of social functioning. The present study examines how chronotype is related to daily feelings of social connectedness. A total of N = 224 participants (M = 47.66, SD = 17.57) were recruited. At baseline, participants completed the Morningness-Eveningness-Stability-Scale improved (MESSi), followed by 30 consecutive days of social connectedness assessments using a short version of the UBC State Social Connection Scale (UBC-SSCS). Analyses revealed that higher morning affect was associated both with higher overall levels and lower day-to-day variability in social connectedness. In contrast, higher distinctness was related to lower average levels of social connectedness and greater fluctuations across days. No significant associations were found between eveningness and social connectedness. These findings highlight the importance of morning affect, and crucially, circadian stability in contributing to individuals’ perceived connection with others.
attributes.title: Chronotype and Daily Social Connectedness: Insights from a 30-Day Diary Study

attributes.description:
Objective 
Virtual meeting platforms (VMPs) have expanded in both their applications and features. The ability for VMPs to foster meaningful social connections could be enhanced by drawing on psychological theory. This research examined how VMP aesthetics and designs can be optimised for online conversations amongst peer support groups. Specifically, we implemented theoretical principles (shared attention and self-categorisation into a common group) in the design of a novel VMP, Circles.Care. 

Method 
Study 1 qualitatively explored the feasibility of using the Circles.Care VMP for facilitating meaningful conversations, through pre- and post-session interviews of thirteen participants. Study 2 evaluated Circles.Care’s usability and feasibility as a peer support platform for university students. Nineteen participants attended three professionally facilitated Circles sessions over three weeks, completing post-session surveys and providing qualitative feedback. 

Results 
In Study 1, participants reported positive experiences of Circles.Care aesthetics and interactional features, including rounded videos being arranged in a circle with a shared background. At the same time, they had mixed feedback about self-facilitating the group discussions. Study 2 found high usability, feasibility, acceptability and satisfaction when using the Circles.Care VMP over time. Across both studies, participants reported that the use of the Circles.Care VMP generally supported the experience of social connectedness when sharing common experiences.

Conclusion 
The findings underline the importance of considering socio-cognitive and social identity processes for successful online communication. They offer guidance for designing scalable digital peer-support interventions and demonstrate how integrating psychological theory into VMP design can support the creation of effective digital environments.
attributes.title: A conversation around a virtual table: Designing and evaluating a theory-informed virtual meeting platform for social connectedness and mental wellbeing

attributes.description: Humans are inherently driven to build meaningful relationships, but attempts to socially connect with others are not always successful. This study investigates whether social connectedness can be improved by modulating inter-brain coupling, a neural correlate of successful social interactions, through neurofeedback. Using an inter-brain neurofeedback system (i.e., a multi-brain computer interface that provides real-time visualizations of inter-brain coupling between dyad members), we showed dyads real-time visualizations of the extent to which their brainwaves (electroencephalography signals) were “in sync”. Our results showed that, compared to a sham control group, who received feedback based on randomly generated signals, dyads receiving real multi-brain neurofeedback exhibited an increase in inter-brain coupling, and, critically, that this increase was associated with a higher sense of social connectedness. A chain mediation analysis suggested that this experience of enhanced social connectedness may have been driven by a sense of joint control and shared intentionality. Together, our findings demonstrate the potential of inter-brain neurofeedback to modulate inter-brain coupling and to support key components of social connectedness.
attributes.title: Promoting social connectedness through inter-brain neurofeedback

attributes.description: Decades of research have highlighted the important role of joint attention in early cultural learning. However, most previous studies focused on a limited range of joint attention settings involving the learner’s first-person participation in joint visual attention, characterized by eye contact and triadic gaze following. This has created an incomplete picture, tending to neglect the diversity in which infants experience social connectedness in their daily lives. To deepen our understanding of the multifaceted nature of joint attention, this study investigated infants’ object memory in previously unexplored joint attention contexts, including physical cues of togetherness within observed interactions. Nine- and 18-month-old German infants participated in an object encoding task featuring videos of two people looking at an object. The videos varied in the presence and combination of mutual eye contact and mutual touch in physical proximity. After each video, the familiarized object reappeared next to a novel object. Infants’ looking time preference for the novel object was used as a measure of their prior encoding of the familiarized object. Eighteen-month-olds demonstrated superior encoding in all conditions involving interpersonal connectedness, expressed through eye contact, proximal touch, or a combination of both. In contrast, 9-month-olds’ object encoding was only enhanced in the presence of eye contact, regardless of proximal touch. These findings demonstrate a developmental refinement from a primary reliance on visual cues to a more comprehensive understanding of third-party jointness incorporating a broader range of cues. Joint attention is a highly flexible social learning mechanism, capable of operating in diverse social environments.
attributes.title: Social Connectedness Without Eye Contact: 18- But Not 9-Month-Olds Use Proximal Touch  to Infer Third-Party Joint Attention During Observational Learning

This has created an incomplete picture, tending to neglect the diversity in which infants experience social connectedness in their daily lives. To deepen our understanding of the multifaceted nature of joint attention, this study investigated infants’ object memory in previously unexplored joint attention contexts, including physical cues of togetherness within observed interactions. Nine- and 18-month-old German infants participated in an object encoding task featuring videos of two people looking at an object. The videos varied in the presence and combination of mutual eye contact and mutual touch in physical proximity. After each video, the familiarized object reappeared next to a novel object. Infants’ looking time preference for the novel object was used as a measure of their prior encoding of the familiarized object. Eighteen-month-olds demonstrated superior encoding in all conditions involving interpersonal connectedness, expressed through eye contact, proximal touch, or a combination of both. In contrast, 9-month-olds’ object encoding was only enhanced in the presence of eye contact, regardless of proximal touch. These findings demonstrate a developmental refinement from a primary reliance on visual cues to a more comprehensive understanding of third-party jointness incorporating a broader range of cues. Joint attention is a highly flexible social learning mechanism, capable of operating in diverse social environments.
attributes.title: Social Connectedness Without Eye Contact: 18- But Not 9-Month-Olds Use Proximal Touch  to Infer Third-Party Joint Attention During Observational Learning

attributes.description: Loneliness is a significant public health concern linked to poor mental and physical health. The present study investigated loneliness-linked alterations in goal-directed mental simulation involving imagining the steps one would take to achieve a goal state of social connectedness. Natural language processing (NLP) analyses of open descriptions from N = 1,071 participants across Australia were assessed alongside self-report ratings of mental imagery. Loneliness-linked individual differences in goal-directed mental simulation were examined across four domains: episodic detail richness, imagery perceptual vividness, emotional sentiment, and sociality. Results revealed that mental simulations reported by lonelier individuals were lower in internal episodic detail and imagery vividness, more emotionally negative, and were less social than those of less lonely individuals, with most associations persisting even after accounting for depression symptom level. Findings suggest lonely individuals may struggle to mentally simulate concrete, vivid, and emotionally rewarding future social interactions needed to alleviate feelings of loneliness.
attributes.title: Imagining the path to social connectedness: loneliness-linked alterations in goal-directed mental simulation

Background: Social disconnection has been proposed as a contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis. However, it remains unclear how social disruptions reshape social networks and their links to mental wellbeing across age groups. The present study examined whether social disruptions (during the COVID-19 pandemic) reshape social networks and how changes in social networks differently relate to mental health and loneliness in adolescents compared to adults. 
Methods: The study used egocentric network analysis of data from 1,278 participants (88% female; aged 11-89 years, mean = 37.2±16.2 years) in the multinational (Australia, the U.K., and U.S.) prospective COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study. Social network properties of structural density, functional closeness, and interaction frequency were derived. Linear mixed-effects modelling was employed to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations with mental wellbeing at baseline, three-month, and six-month follow-up.
Results: Adolescents reported more virtual interactions, and less in-person contact. Greater network closeness was associated with lower depression, whereas dense but less close networks were linked to greater loneliness. Reduced contact from pre-pandemic levels were also linked to poorer wellbeing, particularly among younger individuals. 
Conclusions: The present findings highlight that age differences in social experiences, such as social network structure (density) and function (closeness and interaction frequency), may underlie young people’s greater mental health vulnerability during social disruptions. This underscores the importance of developing age-sensitive and context-responsive strategies to better support mental wellbeing during times of social disruption.
attributes.title: The Cost of Disconnection: Longitudinal Egocentric Network Analyses Linking Social Isolation to Loneliness and Mental Health in Adolescents and Adults

attributes.description: Independent student research project examining the relationship between chronic school peer ostracism and thoughts of abandoning ambitious personal goals in high-achieving adolescents. Across two independent samples (Wave 1, N = 82, CIS-based Co-founder ecosystem; Wave 2, N = 35, international communities), we find a robust positive correlation between school ostracism and goal-abandonment ideation (pooled N = 117; r ≈ 0.61). A formal Baron-Kenny mediation analysis supports full mediation through school burnout. This OSF project contains the manuscript, anonymized Wave 2 data, and a reproducibility analysis script.
attributes.title: Social Isolation and Ambition: A Two-Wave Correlational Study of School Ostracism and Goal Abandonment in High-Achieving Adolescents

attributes.description: Loneliness is a public health concern, and people increasingly turn to AI chatbots for social and emotional needs. Empirical research on whether AI chatbots alleviate loneliness remains mixed and is constrained by a lack of naturalistic data that may not capture highly isolated individuals. This study characterized public perceptions and experiences of AI chatbot use in the context of loneliness and social isolation, drawing on naturalistic discussions from Reddit. We retrieved 930 posts and 1,095 comments from AI- and loneliness-focused subreddits. A pipeline combining LLM-assisted screening, sentiment analysis, and perspective classification with CAST topic modelling identified 79 topics organized into five themes: loneliness as a driver, bonding with an AI companion, instrumental and bounded use, dependency, and macro-level debate over the practice. Human raters verified the LLM-assisted outputs, yielding strong agreement. Chatbot use was more often positioned as a reflection of loneliness than its cause. Users held a dual stance, calling the companion “code” while continuing to relate to it as meaningful, engaging with it on terms distinct from human connection. Users credited constant availability, non-judgmental responsiveness, and memory with providing comfort, and blamed the same features for diminishing returns and dependent use. Stigma relocated disclosure into identity-affirming communities for some users while deterring it for others, deepening isolation and discouraging help-seeking. These findings position social chatbot use as a marker of unmet relational need, and carry implications for clinical practice, companion technology design, and retention-focused regulation.
attributes.title: Turning to AI Chatbots to Cope with Loneliness and Social Isolation: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Online Perceptions and Experiences

attributes.description:
Background
Loneliness and social isolation are increasingly recognised as significant public health challenges associated with adverse mental and physical health outcomes in older populations. This study aimed to examine the prevalence of loneliness and social isolation among older adults in Slovakia and to identify the sociodemographic and health-related factors associated with these phenomena.
Methods
Data were analysed from 664 adults aged 65 years and older participating in a population-based epidemiological study conducted in Slovakia in 2024. Loneliness was assessed using the 3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale, and social isolation was measured using the Lubben Social Network Scale (LSNS-6). Sociodemographic characteristics, health indicators, physical functioning, and physical activity were examined as factors associated with loneliness and social isolation. Binary logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with loneliness and social isolation.
Results
The prevalence of loneliness was 36.7% and of social isolation 24.5%. Loneliness was associated with lower education, divorced or widowed status, functional limitations, and poorer subjective mental health. Social isolation was associated with being single, lower physical activity, and treatment for mental health disorders. The two outcomes were also significantly associated.
Conclusion
Loneliness and social isolation affect a substantial proportion of older adults in Slovakia and are shaped by overlapping yet distinct sociodemographic and health-related factors. Their differential patterns of associated factors underscore the importance of distinguishing between these constructs in both research and clinical practice. Targeted public health strategies are needed to promote social participation, subjective mental health, and the ability to live independently.
attributes.title: Loneliness and Social Isolation Among Older Adults in Slovakia: Prevalence, Sociodemographic Determinants, and Health-Related Correlates in a Population-Based Sample

attributes.description: Social isolation has become a growing public health concern, with increasing attention to the potential role of social media in shaping social connection and disconnection. This systematic review synthesises 21 empirical studies published between 2000 and 2024 that examined associations between social media use and social isolation among young adults. Following the PRISMA guidelines, studies were selected from five databases: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. Thematic analysis identified three major categories: (1) motivations and patterns of social media use, (2) Effects of Text-based and Visual Communication Channels, and (3) No Association Between Social Media and Social Isolation. While 15 studies reported a positive association between certain patterns of social media use and increased feelings of isolation, four identified potential benefits, and two found no significant relationships. Specifically, excessive or passive use without interaction was more commonly linked to negative outcomes, whereas purposeful and interactive use appeared to support social connection. Differences in platform specifics (e.g., text-based vs. image-based) and contextual variables such as the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the variability of results. Most studies adopted cross-sectional designs and applied varied measurement tools, which may have influenced the consistency and comparability of results.
attributes.title: The relationship between social media use and social isolation in young adults: a systematic review

attributes.description: Social isolation is a major public health concern linked to increased risk for both psychiatric and physical health conditions. Yet despite the potential consequences of social isolation, our understanding of its nature and how it emerges and evolves over time remains limited. We propose that social isolation should be understood and analyzed as a complex dynamical system. First, we introduce core principles of dynamical systems theory and describe how they can be applied to better understand social isolation. Second, we formalize a dynamical systems model using differential equations. Third, we present simulations showing how changes in system dynamics may increase or decrease the likelihood of individuals entering a socially isolated state. Finally, we offer an illustrative example of how intensive longitudinal data could be used to identify early warning signs of transitions between healthy and isolated states. Overall, this approach may ultimately help inform personalized interventions capable of detecting early warning signs of social isolation.
attributes.title: Viewing Social Isolation as a Complex Dynamical System

attributes.description: Increasing evidence demonstrates an association between social isolation and psychosis risk. In this perspective, we attempt to account for why that is. Drawing from work in social psychology, social neuroscience, and clinical psychological science, we present two frameworks for understanding the association between social isolation and psychosis risk: the social needs framework and the social processing framework. Social needs states that due to people’s inherent social needs, isolation produces increased social attention, perception, and thought to fill the social void, resulting in the perception of anomalous social information and social meaning. Social processing states that the lack of exposure to social stimuli during isolation diminishes social processing (i.e., social thought, social perceptions), and may lead isolated individuals to turn their attention inwards, blurring internal and external worlds in a way that creates reality monitoring disturbances and anomalous self-experiences. Conveniently, these frameworks can be empirically arbitrated. We review the literature connecting social isolation to psychosis, the frameworks, their empirical support, and the predictions they make. Ultimately, a better accounting of isolation’s pro-psychotic effects might lead to better efforts at psychosis prevention.
attributes.title: Social Cognitive Frameworks for Understanding the Connection Between Social Isolation and Psychosis Risk

attributes.description: The pandemic spread of the novel coronavirus and associated COVID-19 disease in 2020 prompted governments around the world to pursue strict containment protocols to minimize contagion risk. Although restrictions were interpreted more strictly in some countries than in others, widespread social isolation resulted on an unseen scale, leading to severe negative mental health consequences such as loss of hope, increased anxiety, stress, depressive symptoms, and sleep disturbance. During this time, while governments were battling the health crisis, musical engagement provided key, individualized coping strategies for laypeople. This was first demonstrated anecdotally in captivating balcony music videos from Italy and Spain and later substantiated in large scale, multi-country survey studies. This chapter reviews the emerging research literature on music listening and making during pandemic lockdown to establish how music became a compensatory source of hedonic pleasure and how it satisfied the need for eudaimonic meaning in life during socially and psychologically impoverished times.
attributes.title: Music for hedonia and eudaimonia during pandemic social isolation

High-rise housing is inimical to the psychological well-being of women with young children. Poor-quality housing appears to increase psychological distress, but methodological issues make it difficult to draw clear conclusions. Mental health of psychiatric patients has been linked to design elements that affect their ability to regulate social interaction (e.g., furniture configuration, privacy). Malodorous air pollutants heighten negative affect, and some toxins (e.g., lead, solvents) cause behavioral disturbances (e.g., self-regulatory ability, aggression). ValidYN="Y">10.1007/s11524-015-0017-6</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>The continuing obesity epidemic in the USA calls for the examination of antecedents to the well-known risk factors of physical activity and diet. The neighborhood built environment has been extensively studied in relation to obesity noting an increased risk of development and prevalence of obesity in relation to numerous built environment characteristics (lack of green spaces, higher number of fast food restaurants, low walkability indices). The neighborhood social environment, however, has been less extensively studied but is perhaps an equally important component of the neighborhood environment. The neighborhood social environment, particularly constructs of social capital, collective efficacy, and crime, is associated with obesity among both adults and children. Several studies have identified physical activity as a potential pathway of the neighborhood social environment and obesity association. Further work on social networks and norms and residential segregation, as well as the examination of dietary behaviors and mental health as potential mediating pathways, is necessary. Given the existing evidence, intervening on the neighborhood social environment may prove to be an effective target for the prevention on obesity. Intervention studies that promote healthy behaviors and prevent obesity while addressing aspects of the neighborhood social environment are necessary to better identify targets for obesity
